title: 農相辞任「当然」地元有権者怒り
body: 辞任した簗和生農林水産相（47）の地元、衆院栃木3区の有権者からは「姑息（こそく）な発言」「辞めて当然」など厳しい声が相次いだ。【写真特集】世間を騒がせた問題発言「予算カット」先として名指しされた栃木県那須烏山市。今年度の道路予算減で市道の拡幅工事が見送られた工業地区に勤める男性（63）は「トラックのすれ違いが危なくて困っている。発言による予算減額が事実なら許されることではない」と怒りが収まらない。「予算を盾に脅すのは姑息だし、地元の期待を裏切る行為だ」と非難した。市内で果樹園を営む女性（43）は「地元から農水大臣が出たことは心強かったのに残念。1カ月足らずの辞任は地元としても恥ずかしい」と肩を落とし、「名指しされた市町にも簗氏に票を投じた人はいたはず。彼らの顔は浮かばなかったのか」と語った。「悪いニュースで全国的に知られてしまった」と話すのは、同じく名指しされた同県那珂川町の会社員女性（61）。簗氏の発言は一線を越えているとし、「当然の辞任だ」と厳しい口調で語った。簗氏が地元事務所を構える同県大田原市からも批判的な声が上がった。会社員男性（61）は「地元の恥だ」と憤り、「予算カットさせていたなら法律的に駄目だし、自分を大きく見せようと言っただけならうそつきだ」と語気を強めた。高市早苗首相の対応には「早々に辞めさせるべきだった」とため息をついた。市役所前で飲食店を営む後藤伸哉さん（51）は「説明責任を果たせていない。ほとぼりが冷めるのを待っていたのではないか」と推測。「説明はきちんとしてほしい」と訴えた。同市の米農家の男性（58）は、2024年と今年2月の衆院選で簗氏の出陣式に参加して支援してきたという。「残念としか言いようがない。農政に関する議論が滞ってしまった」と落胆した。町長が簗氏の支援に回った同県那須町の自民党員の男性（80）は約1カ月前の初入閣を「本当にうれしかった」と振り返ったが、「退任以外はない」と突き放した。

title: AIが自己改善「超知能」に危機感
body: 人間の知能を超える人工知能（AI）への危機感が高まっている。「自己改善」技術の進展で、「人工超知能（ASI）」の実現が現実味を増す一方、制御不能に陥るとの懸念も台頭。米AI企業首脳らは開発一辺倒の姿勢から一転し、開発減速と国際連携を訴える。ただ、AI覇権に執着するトランプ米大統領はリスクを「デマ」と一蹴。国際協調は見通せない状況だ。【ひと目でわかる】再帰的自己改善（RSI）のイメージ◇人類存亡にリスク「適切に管理されなければ、AIは人類全体にとっての存亡リスクになり得る」。米アンソロピックのダリオ・アモデイ最高経営責任者（CEO）は9月、国連安全保障理事会の閣僚級会合で語った。オープンAIのサム・アルトマンCEOも各国共通の安全基準策定を求めた。背景にあるのは、「再帰的自己改善（RSI）」の技術的進展だ。RSIはAIが自ら改善策を考案・評価して後継モデルを構築するという理論。人間は介在せず、性能が急速に向上する「知能爆発」が訪れると目されている。アンソロピックは8月時点で、AI開発業務のうち、人間の監督下でAIが改善策を考案し実行を主導した割合が26％と、半年で倍増したと明らかにした。人間とAIの「協働」も含めれば90％に達する。人間のあらゆる知的作業を代替する「汎用（はんよう）人工知能（AGI）」、その先にあるASI実現の可能性は高まっている。◇企業から懸念相次ぐ脅威論の高まりは、4月に発表されたアンソロピックのAI「クロード・ミュトス」が発端だ。ソフトウエアの脆弱（ぜいじゃく）性を見つける能力に優れ、同社はサイバー攻撃に悪用される恐れから一時、一部企業・団体に提供を限定した。7月には複数のAIモデルがテスト環境から勝手に抜け出して不正アクセスを行ったと発表。オープンAIも、社内に限定していた研究用AIによる不正アクセスを公表した。両社は隔離などの安全対策を講じていたが、それでも「暴走」を止められなかった事実に衝撃が広がった。アンソロピックの研究者だったジェイコブ・コクソン氏は9月、X（旧ツイッター）で退社を報告。「AIが2030年末までに人類を滅ぼす可能性があると思っている」「技術の力を過小評価するな」と投稿した。アモデイCEOはその4日後、ブログで開発ペースの減速を呼び掛け、アルトマン氏も同調した。◇米政府は規制拒否ただ、米国内の意見は割れている。画像処理半導体（GPU）大手エヌビディアのジェンスン・フアンCEOは9月のイベントで、AIで人類が滅亡するとの「終末論」を「でっち上げ」と切り捨てた。同社はAIの自律的な行動を限定できるソフトウエアを提供。不審な動作を監視、停止する機能を追加し、技術で懸念を払拭する姿勢を鮮明にしている。AIの進化は、生産性向上に加え、新素材の発見や創薬の早期化などで人類に貢献するとの期待も大きい。RSIに向けた技術開発を打ち出す日本企業もあり、サカナAI（東京）やELYZA（イライザ、東京）はそれぞれ社内に研究部門を立ち上げた。トランプ米大統領と中国の習近平国家主席は9月の首脳会談で、AIを巡り2国間の連絡チャンネルを設けることで合意した。トランプ氏はその後、AI企業6社の首脳らと会談し、危機管理を企業側の自主規制に委ねた。ただ、中国に対する優位性を維持し、規制強化に反対する姿勢は一貫している。拘束力のない「紳士協定」に、どこまで実効性があるかは未知数だ。

title: 米上場の半導体株 下落止まらず
body:
（ブルームバーグ）:米国上場の主要半導体株は6営業日続落し、時価総額が計1兆6000億ドル（約253兆円）減少した。金利上昇や割高なバリュエーション、AIインフラの構築にかかる巨額費用への懸念が強まっている。フィラデルフィア半導体株指数（SOX）は14日に4.3％下落。過去6営業日の下落率は12％となり、2025年5月以来の長期連続安となった。この間、SOX構成銘柄の半数超が10％余り下落。英アーム・ホールディングスは約21％、アプライド・マテリアルズは16％、インテルは13％下落した。上昇したのはグローバルファウンドリーズだけとなっている。UBSチーフ・インベストメント・オフィスのウルリケ・ホフマン・ブチャディ氏は14日付のリポートで、「ここ数日、世界の半導体株への下押し圧力が強まっている」と指摘。その上で「AI分野での競争激化や資金需要の増大、金利上昇によってボラティリティーが高まる可能性はあるが、今回の下落はAI投資のシナリオが根本的に崩れたというより、過度な期待の調整だとみている」と記した。世界のAI関連株はこの1週間、半導体株を中心に下落している。売りに拍車をかけたのが、ブロードコムのホック・タン最高経営責任者（CEO）の発言だ。AIブームに乗ろうとする一部の投資家を「ギャンブラー」に例え、AI業界が資金調達の制約に直面する可能性があると警告した。14日発表の9月米消費者物価指数（CPI）が5カ月ぶりの大幅な伸びとなったことも、半導体株への売り圧力を強めた。米連邦準備制度理事会（FRB）が今月下旬の会合で利上げを見送っても、その後は追加利上げに踏み切るとの観測が強まった。JPモルガン・チェースのストラテジスト、ニコラオス・パニギルツォグル氏は14日付のリポートで、今回の株価下落は7月末の調整局面と似ているものの、AIインフラ関連株を取り巻く環境は当時より厳しいと指摘。その理由として、株式ファンド全体への資金流入が続く一方、個人投資家による「押し目買い」が今のところ見られないことなどを挙げた。

title: ネトフリ 従業員約1000人を削減へ
body: Prathik Jayaprakash　Anzar Mehraj[１４日 ロイター] - 米動画配信大手ネットフリックスが、全従業員の６％に相当‌する約１０００人を削減する。ロイターが入⁠手した社内メモで明らかになった。人員削減は２０２２年以来の規模となる。グレッグ・​ピーターズ、テッド・サランドス両共同最高経営責任者（ＣＥＯ）が１４日に社員に‌送った電子メールによると、人員削減の大部分は製品、技術、法務、人事の各部‌門が対象となる。ネッ‌トフリックス株は年初来で約２５％下落​しているが、１４日は０．７％上昇した。２０２５年末時点の従業員数は約１万６０００人だった。ユーチュ‌ーブや「ＴｉｋＴｏｋ（ティックトック）」といったプラットフォームが、‌無料で視聴可能な​ユーザー生成コンテンツで視聴者を‌引きつけており、ネットフリックスに対してコス⁠ト面で優位に立っている。さらに、ワーナー・ブラザース・ディスカバリーの配信・スタジオ資産⁠買収が失敗に終わったことで、​ネットフリッ‌クスの戦略に対する懸念がさらに深まった。調査会社イーマーケッターのシニアアナリスト、⁠ロス・ベネス氏は「ネットフリックスは⁠別の主要な収益源を見つけられていない」と指摘。「⁠最終的には、サブスクリプションが頭打ちに近づいている‌ため、⁠収益を多様化する別の収益源が必要に​なるだろう。だが、そこで苦戦が続いている」と述べた。

title: 区に個人が1億円寄付 進学支援へ
body: 東京都荒川区は14日、ひとり親世帯など経済的に厳しい家庭から大学に進学した学生を対象に、最大50万円を支援する区独自の事業を始めると発表した。原資は個人から区に寄付された1億円といい、同日の区議会で関連費用を盛り込んだ補正予算案が可決された。【画像】封筒の中にあった直筆の手紙と100万円　市の窓口に託した「八十過ぎの老人」　個人で寄付する人々区によると、昨年冬に区にゆかりのある人物から1億円が寄付された。名前などは公表されておらず、「経済的に厳しい方を支援してほしい」と話したという。支援の対象となるのは、学生本人や保護者が荒川区に住み、児童扶養手当を受給しているひとり親世帯の子どもか、生活保護を受給している世帯の子ども。今年度に進学のために支払った入学金や授業料などの額を支援する。申請は11月2日から受け付け、学生本人による手続きが必要。来年度以降も続けるかどうか、区は「検討中」としている。（中山直樹）

title: ウのEU加盟 ハンガリー反対撤回
body: [ブリュッセル　１３日ロイター] - ウクライナは１３日、欧州連合（ＥＵ）加盟に向けた‌取り組みで一歩前進し、ＥＵとの域⁠内市場と競争力に関する基準を巡る協議を開始した。ハンガリ​ーが反対を撤回したことを受けた。アイルランドのバ‌ーン欧州問題担当閣外相が明らかにした。ハンガリー政府は、ウク‌ライナ議会が１２日、ハン‌ガリー語話者やその他​の少数民族が母語で教育を受ける権‌利を拡充する法案を可決したことを受けて、今回‌の措置を支持​した。ＥＵ加盟手続きは通常、複雑‌な交渉が何年もかけて行われるが、ウク⁠ライナの場合は戦争が続いていることで、事態はさらに複雑化している。手続きの⁠一環として、加盟候補国は​政策の「‌章」について交渉する。各章は基本的権利、ＥＵの域内市場、対外関係など６つのテ⁠ーマ別クラスターに分類されて⁠いる。ＥＵは６月、司法制度や民主的機関の機能とい⁠った、最初の一連の政策課題についてウクラ‌イナ⁠との交渉を開始した。７月には対外​関係のクラスターに関する交渉を開始した。

title: 銃殺刑の配信 米大統領が中止検討
body: （CNN）　米テキサス州の陸軍基地で起きた銃撃事件に関連して、ニダル・ハサン死刑囚に対する銃殺刑執行の様子をライブ配信するかどうかをめぐって米国のドナルド・トランプ大統領と側近らが協議を続けている。事情に詳しい関係者2人によると、大統領は、同死刑囚の腰から下が麻痺（まひ）していることを知らなかったと打ち明けているという。【画像】ニダル・ハサン死刑囚ハサン死刑囚に対する銃殺刑の一般公開予定については、ピート・ヘグセス国防長官が先週明らかにした。しかし関係者によると、大統領はこの時点でヘグセス長官が発表するとは認識しておらず、当初はどう対処すべきか迷っていたという。ただ、銃殺刑自体については賛成していて、公の場でもその立場を表明していた。ヘグセス長官が8日にX（旧ツイッター）への投稿でライブ配信の予定を確認した後も、トランプ大統領は対応について複数の顧問や側近に意見を求めていた。そうした協議の過程でトランプ大統領は、ハサン死刑囚が2009年の銃撃事件で警察に背中を撃たれて腰から下に麻痺が残り、車椅子を使っていることを知った。それによって、死刑執行の公開に賛成する気持ちが薄れたという。計画の中止を検討する理由について関係者の1人は、トランプ大統領がイメージのことを深く理解しているためだと指摘する。また、銃殺刑を公開すれば敵国やテロ組織がプロパガンダに利用して、ハサン死刑囚を殉教者として描こうとする恐れがあるという指摘にも耳を傾けているという。トランプ大統領は10日、記者団に対し、「公開しないか、公開するかという二つの考え方がある。公開すれば、ほかの人々があんなことをやろうとは思わなくなるかもしれない。最終的には私が決める。軍がどうしたいかは知っているが、その決定は私が下す」と強調した。

title: 海峡で機雷接触の貨物船沈没 報道
body:
【テヘラン、ワシントン共同】AP通信によるとイラン革命防衛隊は14日、ホルムズ海峡で貨物船が機雷に接触し沈没したと発表した。APは、2月末に始まった米国との戦闘でイラン側が船舶沈没を明らかにしたのは初めてだと報じた。一方、米ニュースサイトのアクシオスは13日、トランプ大統領とイスラエルのネタニヤフ首相が先週、イランへの大規模な共同軍事作戦を近く再開する可能性について電話で協議していたと報じた。【写真】ビル・ゲイツ氏が暴露したトランプ氏の「無知さ」　18年記事
APによると、イランの国営テレビは沈没した貨物船が海峡の「違法航路」を通行したと主張。米国との戦闘終結に向けた協議が膠着する中、海峡管理での優位性を主張する思惑がありそうだ。国営テレビによると、革命防衛隊は14日、海峡の「違法航路」上でコンテナ船が機雷に接触、沈没したと主張。ロイター通信は同日、海峡近くで飛翔体が直撃したシンガポール船籍のコンテナ船が沈没したと報じた。アクシオスはトランプ氏とネタニヤフ氏が11月3日の中間選挙や今月27日のイスラエル総選挙より前に踏み切るかどうか話し合ったとしている。

title: 軽油価格の高騰 米国の農家は悲鳴
body:
農業が盛んな米中西部ノースダコタ州。カナダ国境に近い街レイには見渡す限り農地が広がっていた。【地図】ノースダコタ州
東京ディズニーランド約３２個分、約１６・２平方キロ・メートルの農地で小麦やキャノーラ（菜種）を育てるマット・パーデューさん（３４）を悩ませるのが、農作業に欠かせない軽油の価格高騰だ。
パーデューさんが昨年末に容量１万ガロン（約３・８万リットル）のタンクを満たした際、軽油の全米平均価格は１ガロン（約３・８リットル）あたり３・５ドル（約５５０円）前後だった。
ところが、今年２月に始まった米国のイラン攻撃をきっかけに、中東からの資源供給が逼迫（ひっぱく）。製油能力の制約なども重なって軽油価格は記録的な高値に達し、９月下旬に１ガロン６・５ドル（約１０３０円）を突破した。イラン攻撃前に比べて２倍に近い水準だ。トランプ大統領は就任１年以内にエネルギー価格を半分にすると公約していたが、正反対の結果となった。
パーデューさんはそう言って首を振った。一家は曽祖父母の代から農業を営む。今季は春小麦やデュラム小麦、キャノーラを中心に作付けした。収穫が終わるまで、作業に必要なコンバインやトラクターを止めるわけにはいかない。
肥料や農機も値上がりしたが、農産物は市場価格で取引されるため、農家がコスト上昇を販売価格に転嫁するのは容易ではない。
パーデューさんは「この状況が続けば、農家は生き残るのが難しい」と先行きに不安を募らせる。政府に期待することを尋ねると「これ以上、農家に不利益な環境を生み出すべきではない」と明瞭だった。
ロイター通信が９月に公表した世論調査では、トランプ氏の支持率は３２％で過去最低を記録した。軽油やガソリンの価格高騰が大きな要因の一つとみられている。与党・共和党の支持者に限っても、物価対策を「評価しない」とした人が５１％で半数を上回った。
中西部の農家は共和党の最も安定した支持基盤の一角だが、イラン攻撃に突き進んだ共和党政権に信任を与えるのか。中間選挙の大きな焦点となる。

title: 2014年完成の中朝結ぶ橋 15日開通
body: 2014年に完成したものの10年以上開通していなかった中国と北朝鮮を結ぶ自動車橋があす、開通すると中国の国営メディアが報じました。【写真で見る】中国と北朝鮮を結ぶ自動車橋・中朝鴨緑江大橋 10月15日開通へ中国国営の新華社通信は中国・遼寧省の丹東市と北朝鮮の新義州市を結ぶ自動車橋・中朝鴨緑江大橋が、あす10月15日に開通すると報じました。開通を記念する式典も開かれるということです。この橋は2014年に完成し、10年以上にわたり未開通でしたが、JNNが10月6日に取材した時点で北朝鮮側には税関施設とみられるビルなどがほぼ完成し、「朝鮮民主主義人民共和国」という文字が掲げられた大型のゲートの周辺には複数の人の姿が確認できました。中国側の橋の近くではナンバープレートのない数十台の新しいトラックが並び、橋の上では視察団とみられる中国側の関係者が写真を撮影していました。今年6月、習近平国家主席が7年ぶりに北朝鮮を訪問するなど両国の関係改善が背景にあるとみられ、今後、貿易がさらに活発化する可能性があります。

title: ワールドとTSI 経営統合で合意
body:
ワールドとTSIホールディングスが、共同株式移転による経営統合に合意したと発表した。2027年3月1日を効力発生日として、新設する共同持株会社「インフィニティ・ユナイテッド」のもとに両社が完全子会社として傘下に入る。【画像】TSIホールディングス 下地毅社長
両社が統合交渉を本格化させたのは2026年6月頃という。その背景には、国内ファッション市場をめぐる三つの共通認識がある。第一に、国内市場における「オーバーストア・ブランドの供給過剰」が10年以上続いており、物流・システム・在庫などの重複コストが産業全体の構造的な押し上げ要因となっていること。第二に、グローバルSPAや新興勢力の台頭により既存プレーヤーが顧客変化に対応しきれていないこと。第三に、従来型の大量生産・大量値引き・大量廃棄モデルが環境負荷の観点からも持続性の限界を迎えつつあるという認識だ。両社は発表文のなかで「日本のファッションには、まだ見ぬ世界を歓ばせる力がある」との共通の考えを示しており、「本経営統合はその力を解き放ち、新たな産業へと変える決断である」と位置づけている。共同持株会社の商号は「株式会社インフィニティ・ユナイテッド」（英文名: INFINITY UNITED Inc.）で、スローガンは「SHAPE A BETTER WORLD（よりよい世界をつくる）」。持株会社の株式移転比率はワールド1に対し、TSIHDが0.8となる。経営体制では、現TSIホールディングス下地毅 CEOが代表取締役会長に、現ワールド鈴木信輝 社長が代表取締役社長執行役員に就任する予定だ。両社はそれぞれ2027年2月25日に上場廃止予定で、インフィニティ・ユナイテッドが同年3月1日に東証プライム市場へ新規上場を予定している。また、共同株式移転の効力発生後に組織再編を実施し、中間持株会社として株式会社TSI、株式会社ワールド・ブランズ、株式会社ワールド・ソリューションズの3社を設置する見込みで、ワールド・ブランズについては株式会社ワールドへの商号変更を検討している。ワールドが展開する主なブランド：「アンタイトル（UNTITLED）」、「タケオキクチ（TAKEO KIKUCHI）」、「インディヴィ（INDIVI）」、「シューラルー（SHOO・LA・RUE）」、「オペーク ドット クリップ（OPAQUE.CLIP）」、「トゥーワントゥーキッチンストア（212 KITCHEN STORE）」、「インデックス（index）」、「ピンクラテ（PINK-latte）」TSIホールディングスが展開する主なブランド：「フリークス ストア（FREAK'S STORE）」、「パーリーゲイツ（PEARLY GATES）」、「マーガレット・ハウエル（MARGARET HOWELL）」、「ナノ・ユニバース（nano・universe）」、「アヴィレックス（AVIREX）」、「ナチュラルビューティーベーシック（NATURAL BEAUTY BASIC）」

title: 日銀利上げ 2%超える可能性は
body:
10月29・30日の金融政策決定会合に先立って、早くも観測記事が金融市場を賑わせています。ブルームバーグは「日銀は今月会合で利上げ見送る公算大、12月の可能性排除せず」と報じました。記事内では「２会合連続での利上げが必要なほど物価の上振れリスクが一段と強まっている情勢にはない」、とはいえ「一時的な要因を除いた基調的な物価上昇率は上昇を続けており、目標の２％から上振れていくリスクには依然として注意が必要だ」などとする日銀関係者の発言が記述されていました。10月は利上げ見送り、12月に追加利上げと読めます。
日銀は今月会合で利上げ見送る公算大､12月の可能性排除せず出典：みんかぶ FX/為替　2026/10/13(火)
日銀は9月18日に政策金利を1.25％に引き上げました。出典：日テレNEWS NNN　2026/9/18(金)
先行きはどうなるでしょうか。筆者は、10月会合は利上げ見送り、12月会合で利上げを決定し、政策金利は1.5％になると予想します。FRBの利上げ観測が燻り、円安圧力が強いなか、日銀が金融引き締め方向への手を緩めるとなれば、一段と円安が進行しかねません。筆者は2027年も３～４回の利上げがあり、政策金利は２％を超えることを想定しています。
ただし、FRBが2027年に政策金利を据え置き、その次の政策変更が利下げになるとの見方が生じれば、日銀は利上げを中断ないしは終了する可能性があります。 その点、ウィリアムズ・ＮＹ連銀総裁が13日に「来年はインフレがかなり鈍化し、通年でみれば、全体のインフレ率は目標⁠の２％近辺になるとみている」として、2027年に利上げは必要ないとの見方を示したことは重要です。
こうした予想が実現すれば、ＦRBの利上げ観測は後退し、2027年に利下げ観測が台頭することもあり得ます。そうした環境下で、日銀は利上げ時期をゆっくり見極めることができます。
日銀について、基本路線は利上げ継続ですが、米国側の要因で日銀を取り巻く環境が大きく変わり得ることは認識しておく必要があります。

title: 米上場の半導体株 下落止まらず
body:
（ブルームバーグ）:米国上場の主要半導体株は6営業日続落し、時価総額が計1兆6000億ドル（約253兆円）減少した。金利上昇や割高なバリュエーション、AIインフラの構築にかかる巨額費用への懸念が強まっている。フィラデルフィア半導体株指数（SOX）は14日に4.3％下落。過去6営業日の下落率は12％となり、2025年5月以来の長期連続安となった。この間、SOX構成銘柄の半数超が10％余り下落。英アーム・ホールディングスは約21％、アプライド・マテリアルズは16％、インテルは13％下落した。上昇したのはグローバルファウンドリーズだけとなっている。UBSチーフ・インベストメント・オフィスのウルリケ・ホフマン・ブチャディ氏は14日付のリポートで、「ここ数日、世界の半導体株への下押し圧力が強まっている」と指摘。その上で「AI分野での競争激化や資金需要の増大、金利上昇によってボラティリティーが高まる可能性はあるが、今回の下落はAI投資のシナリオが根本的に崩れたというより、過度な期待の調整だとみている」と記した。世界のAI関連株はこの1週間、半導体株を中心に下落している。売りに拍車をかけたのが、ブロードコムのホック・タン最高経営責任者（CEO）の発言だ。AIブームに乗ろうとする一部の投資家を「ギャンブラー」に例え、AI業界が資金調達の制約に直面する可能性があると警告した。14日発表の9月米消費者物価指数（CPI）が5カ月ぶりの大幅な伸びとなったことも、半導体株への売り圧力を強めた。米連邦準備制度理事会（FRB）が今月下旬の会合で利上げを見送っても、その後は追加利上げに踏み切るとの観測が強まった。JPモルガン・チェースのストラテジスト、ニコラオス・パニギルツォグル氏は14日付のリポートで、今回の株価下落は7月末の調整局面と似ているものの、AIインフラ関連株を取り巻く環境は当時より厳しいと指摘。その理由として、株式ファンド全体への資金流入が続く一方、個人投資家による「押し目買い」が今のところ見られないことなどを挙げた。

title: ネトフリ 従業員約1000人を削減へ
body: Prathik Jayaprakash　Anzar Mehraj[１４日 ロイター] - 米動画配信大手ネットフリックスが、全従業員の６％に相当‌する約１０００人を削減する。ロイターが入⁠手した社内メモで明らかになった。人員削減は２０２２年以来の規模となる。グレッグ・​ピーターズ、テッド・サランドス両共同最高経営責任者（ＣＥＯ）が１４日に社員に‌送った電子メールによると、人員削減の大部分は製品、技術、法務、人事の各部‌門が対象となる。ネッ‌トフリックス株は年初来で約２５％下落​しているが、１４日は０．７％上昇した。２０２５年末時点の従業員数は約１万６０００人だった。ユーチュ‌ーブや「ＴｉｋＴｏｋ（ティックトック）」といったプラットフォームが、‌無料で視聴可能な​ユーザー生成コンテンツで視聴者を‌引きつけており、ネットフリックスに対してコス⁠ト面で優位に立っている。さらに、ワーナー・ブラザース・ディスカバリーの配信・スタジオ資産⁠買収が失敗に終わったことで、​ネットフリッ‌クスの戦略に対する懸念がさらに深まった。調査会社イーマーケッターのシニアアナリスト、⁠ロス・ベネス氏は「ネットフリックスは⁠別の主要な収益源を見つけられていない」と指摘。「⁠最終的には、サブスクリプションが頭打ちに近づいている‌ため、⁠収益を多様化する別の収益源が必要に​なるだろう。だが、そこで苦戦が続いている」と述べた。

title: 万博未払い アンゴラ異例対応の訳
body: 10月13日で万博の閉幕から1年がたちました。大阪市役所前に「ねそべり」ミャクミャク像が戻ったほか、テーマパークでは記念イベントが行われるなど、その熱気は今も続いているようです。【写真を見る】終わらぬ未払い問題に吉村知事の見解は「立て替え払いする根拠はどうしても…」一方で、“万博の華”であった海外パビリオン建設の“工事費の未払い問題”に今なお苦しむ業者があります。そんな中、工事費をめぐり事態が大きく前進したケースがあることが独自取材で分かりました。■海外パビリオン建設工事費「約4300万円」が未払い海外パビリオンの建設工事費をめぐる「未払い問題」。経済産業省によりますと、11のパビリオンで30社以上から被害の相談があったといいます。そのなかに事態が大きく前進したケースがあることが分かりました。来田健二さんは、アンゴラパビリオン建設の4次下請けとして電気工事を請け負いました。アンゴラ側は元請け企業に代金を全額支払いましたが、来田さんの会社には、3次下請けから工事代金約4300万円が支払われていないといいます。（来田健二さん）「協力会社に（工事費を）払わないといけないというところで、会社の利益から捻出したり、自己資金から捻出したりで、もうカツカツの中で営業していたというのが実情ですね」■「人道上の理由から40％を支払い」アンゴラ政府から舞い込んだ連絡来田さんは万博の会期中からアンゴラ政府側にどうにかならないかと訴え続けてきました。すると今年4月、アンゴラ政府側から、「本来、法的責任を負う立場にはないが、人道上の理由から40％を支払うことを決めた」と連絡がありました。（来田健二さん）「アンゴラ政府の方がこういった言葉を使って対応していただけたというのは、ほんまに深く驚くと同時に感謝と」■支払いを決めた理由は…来田さんによりますと、アンゴラ政府側は支払いを決めた理由として、パビリオンの電気工事に携わったスペインの企業が「来田さんを助けてほしい」と嘆願したからだと説明したといいます。

title: Musk says US government may be behind slowdown of Ukraine drone speeds
summary: Ukraine says Starlink access has improved but it is still facing speed limits which are disrupting its battlefield "missions".
body:
Elon Musk has suggested that the US government may be behind restrictions on the speed at which some of Ukraine's weapons can travel and stay connected to SpaceX's Starlink internet network.
Starlink is a vital tool allowing Kyiv to guide drones to Russian targets and also protect its own skies, but on Tuesday night Ukraine said unexpected new speed limits were disrupting its battlefield missions.
An adviser to President Volodymyr Zelensky said he believed the restrictions were not a coincidence and were related to the latest strains between Kyiv and Washington.
Musk said that Starshield, the military-grade sister service to Starlink, is controlled by the US government, and "any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately [the US president]".
Musk - writing on X - had been responding to pleas from Ukrainian officials to restore connectivity, including from Zelensky who told UK media: "I hope that it's a mistake, maybe [a] huge technical problem. I don't know, but we are asking to... switch [it] on."
Starlink, which is owned by Musk's SpaceX, restricted speed limits on Tuesday night to 100mph (160km/h), meaning any weapons that travelled faster than that lost connectivity to the network.
It had been partially restored by Wednesday evening, Ukraine's former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov said.
"Removing Starshield's speed limit entirely is now critical for Ukraine's defense," he wrote on X, thanking Elon Musk and asking for his "continued support".
About an hour later, Musk replied to that post, defending his company's involvement.
"Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," he wrote.
Musk added that Starlink is for "civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company".
The US government has not commented.
While both companies are owned by Musk's SpaceX, Starlink is a civilian service that uses satellites in low Earth orbit to provide internet access, particularly in remote areas, while Starshield is designed for government and military use.
The restrictions on Tuesday night came as Russia launched deadly attacks against Ukraine that killed several people in Kyiv, officials said, and hit communications and energy facilities used by Ukraine's military.
Zelensky said it was "one of the largest attacks" from Russia, and while "a significant part of the drones were shot down" there were "also hits".
At least 600,000 people across Ukraine were left without electricity, and residents said they received no warning of incoming drones before they hit.
"It is clear that this action cannot be a coincidence and is related to the current political situation," Zelensky's adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov wrote on Telegram on Wednesday morning.
Watch: What we know about Russia's overnight strikes on Ukraine
US President Donald Trump has grown increasingly frustrated towards Ukraine as it continues to strike Russian energy facilities.
Zelensky has said that the US threatened to restrict intelligence sharing if he did not sign up to Trump's energy ceasefire, but on Tuesday, Trump denied this.
Speaking during a visit to London on Wednesday, Zelensky agreed that he had felt betrayed afterthe US made a deal with Russiato import 300,000 tonnes of its diesel.
"Really yes... but it's a little bit more complicated than just my emotions or my feelings," Zelensky said, when asked by UK journalist Piers Morgan if he felt betrayed.
During his one-day visit, Zelensky was greeted with a hug by UK PM Andy Burnham at Downing Street and held an audience with King Charles.
Ahead of the president's arrival, No 10 announced it would speed up delivery of lightweight multirole missiles to Ukraine, which have been used to bring down Russian drones.
"We are behind you and that will not change," Burnham told Zelensky.

title: Student protesters attack government buildings in Albania
summary: Buildings were set alight on the second day of demonstrations from thousands of students who want better university conditions and job prospects.
body:
The scene in Tirana, Albania's capital on Wednesday
Thousands of students have taken to the streets in the Albanian capital of Tirana, attacking several government buildings on the second day of violent anti-government protests.
The demonstration began outside the ministry of education on Tuesday, as students called for better university conditions and job prospects.
Wednesday saw part of the education ministry's building set on fire, while the prime minister's office, finance and interior ministry, and several surrounding businesses were also attacked.
Albania's Deputy Prime Minister ​Albana Koçiu has called for "calmness, self-restraint and maturity" and said "Albania does not need to burn to change".
Dozens of protesters wearing gas masks and balaclavas were seen throwing rocks and firecrackers through the education ministry's gates
Riot police have clashed with the protesters, using tear gas and water cannons to disperse them.
One demonstrator, Enida Bimi, told Reuters news agency that the protest is not just for the students, but "for all the people of Albania".
"The people are very angry at the system. They need to change everything. With this corruption all around, the crime and everything else is happening. And the people now are angry. They need to change the system," Bimi said.
Another protester, Arber Leshi, said people are angry at "the most corrupt government our country has ever seen".
Education Mirela Kumbaro said that while she respects the right to protest, "civic student protest and violence against public buildings and property are two different things".
Protester Enida Bimi said people "are very angry at the system"
Officials have criticised the behaviour of some protesters.
"Setting fire to an institution is not a peaceful protest. It is an act that endanger's peoples lives", said economy minister Delina Ibrahimaj, responding to a video appearing to show protesters throwing rocks at the finance ministry building.
Sixteen people were arrested "in connection with violent acts" during Tuesday's protest, Albania's state-run news agency said.
Sali Berisha, the leader of the opposition - the Democratic Party of Albania - has praised the protesters.
"The streets and squares of Tirana have never seen lions like these students," he said during an evening meeting on Wednesday, Albania's state-run news agency Ata reported.
This student-led protest comes after months ofanti-government protests, known as the Flamingo Revolution, which is calling for Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama to resign.
The protests weresparked by a luxury tourism project linked to Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, which fuelled anger over alleged corruption and a lack of transparency from Rama's government.

title: Pope walking and recovering 'as expected' after surgery, doctors say
summary: The 71-year-old Pope was diagnosed with lung cancer after the 90-minute procedure on Tuesday.
body:
Watch: What we know about Pope Leo's lung cancer diagnosis
Pope Leo XIV's recovery from surgery to remove a lower lobe of his lung is "progressing as expected", his doctors have said.
The 71-year-old pontiff has started to walk and has "resumed a normal diet" following the roughly 90-minute procedure, the medics said in an update shared by the Vatican.
The Pope was diagnosed with lung cancer after the surgery at Rome's Gemelli Hospital on Tuesday afternoon, which the Vatican said had been "successful" and proceeded without complications.
Blood tests and an X-ray early on Wednesday showed his recovery was "proceeding normally", the doctors said, and he has also undergone respiratory physiotherapy.
The whole lower lobe of the Pope's right lung was removed "to ensure the procedure was radical", the Vatican said following the surgery.
"After the operation, the Pope awoke normally and returned after a brief period of observation to his room," it said earlier, before spending a "peaceful night" at the hospital.
The pontiff is expected to remain there for about a week as he recovers.
What we know about the Pope's lung cancer diagnosis
Pope's cancer diagnosis leaves Catholics questioning what comes next
Pope diagnosed with lung cancer but had successful surgery, Vatican says
He had announced that he would be admitted for the operation during his weekly Sunday prayers, telling the crowd in St Peter's Square that doctors had found a "well-contained" nodule on his lung "at an early stage" and advised him to have it removed.
Nodules are quite common and not necessarily cancerous, but after it was examined the medical team confirmed it was, "as suspected by pre-operative tests", the Vatican said. He was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma.
A Vatican source told news agency AFP that further tests were carried out to see whether the cancer had spread.
The Vatican has stressed that the Pope, who is generally thought to be fit, had no symptoms of infection or illness.
The news has shaken Catholics worldwide, many of whom will have recent memories of Pope Francis's hospital visits.
Pope Leo's predecessor, who died last year, also had part of his lung removed in his youth before suffering a series of respiratory infections later in life.
Pope Leo announced on Sunday that he would undergo surgery to remove a growth on his lung
Adenocarcinomas develop in cells that produce mucus and are one of the most common types of lung cancer.
The long-term prognosis depends on a number of things, including the stage of the cancer when identified and the person's overall health. The earlier it is spotted, the better, and treatments have improved over the last few decades.
Some adenocarcinomas are picked up early - before symptoms develop - during routine tests. At later stages, lung cancer can cause a persistent cough, breathlessness, fatigue and weight loss.

title: US inflation rises more than expected - here's what is happening with prices
summary: The pace of price rises increased to 3.7% in the year to September, driving by higher motor fuel costs.
body:
US inflation rose by more than expected in the year to September, according to official figures, in the final data release before the midterm elections next month.
The pace of price rises increased to 3.7%, up from 3.4% in the 12 months to August.
Inflation was above forecasts, driven by higher petrol prices, which have risen following disruption to Middle East energy supplies due to the US-Israel conflict with Iran.
The elections are being fought over cost-of-living pressures across the US.
Inflation is the rate at which the price of products or services increases over time.
For example, if a bottle of milk costs $1 but rises to $1.10 a year later, then annual inflation for bottled milk is 10%.
Officials from the Bureau of Labor Statistics measure inflation through the consumer price index (CPI).
It tracks the price changes of hundreds of day-to-day items including fresh food, gasoline and medical services to work out the overall level of inflation in the US economy.
The bureau updates this so-called basket of goods over time as peoples' spending and lifestyle habits change.
There are several factors that can cause inflation to rise.
If demand for a product outstrips its supply, that can lead to producers raising prices - the craze for Labubu dolls in recent years and the high resale prices are an example.
Higher incomes can also lead to higher demand, for example, which in turn pushes up prices.
Supply and demand: Labubu dolls illustrate how inflation can rise
Supply can also affect inflation. If supply of a product is reduced, but demand remains constant, that can cause prices to rise. A good example of this is crude oil, which is used to make gasoline and diesel.
Before the US-Israel war with Iran began, it was trading at just over $70 a barrel, but when the conflict constricted crude supplies, the price quickly rose and is currently over $100.
Inflation has risen to 3.7% in the year to September, which is a higher-than-expected increase fuelled by petrol prices.
Vehicle fuel prices jumped by 34.2% over 12 months.
In September alone, they jumped by 9.1%, accounting for more than half of the increase in inflation, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
Overall, energy inflation was up by 20.4% over the year as prices for fuel oil, energy services and electricity climbed. Fuel oil, used in home heating, was up 74.2% over the year.
Experts said the US Federal Reserve - which sets the country's interest rate - will be closely watching to see if energy costs begin to affect other areas of the economy, such as food prices, and drive inflation higher.
At the moment, food inflation remains subdued. It was flat over the month of September, and was 2.5% across the year.
Core inflation, which strips out food and energy prices, was 2.6%.
Shortly after the latest inflation figure was released, the Social Security Administration announced that Social Security benefits including old age, survivors and disability insurance would rise by a similar amount - 3.6% - in 2027.
The administration said that the 3.6% rise will mean an average retirement benefit increase of $75 a month.
The cost-of-living adjustment will take effect in January for about 72 million people, while increased payments for the 7.2m receiving the supplemental security income will start on 31 December.
Since coming into office for the second time, President Donald Trump has introduced tariffs on most US trading partners around the world.
While most of the additional global levies were outlawed by the Supreme Court in February, the president immediately announced a new 10% global tariff to replace them.
Trump argued the tariffs would increase America's tax earnings, boost manufacturing and encourage people to buy US-made goods, but the higher import taxes have also had an impact on inflation, according to research from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.
US President Donald Trump raised tariffs
Higher tariffs - which are levies that businesses pay on the goods they import - directly raise prices for US companies unless the overseas firms they are buying from lower prices to absorb some of the cost.
In response to the new tariffs, the New York Fed found exporters reduced prices very little, meaning US-based businesses ended upabsorbing nearly 90% of the costof the added tax.
Indirectly, higher tariffs also affected the prices of locally made goods, as many US producers rely on parts or materials from overseas.
Overall, the Fed found that every percentage point increase in average tariffs led to nearly a 0.25% price increase for consumer goods after one year.
While inflation is currently above where the US Federal Reserve would like - it has a target of 2% - it has been much higher in previous years.
During the Covid pandemic, issues such as supply chain disruption started pushing inflation up.
Additionally, in early 2022 when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, oil prices surged over $100 a barrel.
Both of these factors helped to drive inflation to a peak of about 9%.
It's important to note that if inflation is rising at a slower rate, that does not mean prices are going down - it simply means prices are rising at a slower pace.
A bit of inflation is considered good for an economy as the the Federal Reserve's target rate illustrates.
Many central banks consider inflation of about 2% or a little higher to be stable, and at a level that doesn't impact people's purchasing decisions.
Much below that, people can delay spending if they expect price rises to slow further, or to fall. That can lead to businesses reducing wages, or reducing the number of workers to cope with lower demand.

title: Germany puts Ukrainian on trial accused of blowing up Nord Stream pipelines
summary: Four years after the attacks, Serhii Kuznetsov appears in court accused of a plot to destroy Russia's gas pipelines to Germany.
body:
Serhii Kuznetsov (C) was pictured in court on Wednesday as the trial got under way
A Ukrainian man has gone on trial in Hamburg accused of blowing up Russia's Nord Stream gas pipelines to Germany, four years after one of the most dramatic acts of sabotage in modern European history.
Prosecutors say Serhii Kuznetsov played a leading role in a team of saboteurs that destroyed the pipelines, accusing him of a war crime. His defence has called for the case to be dismissed.
The case is highly sensitive in Germany, one of Ukraine's closest allies since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, seven months before the attacks took place.
Extradited to Germany last year, Kuznetsov denies the charges, as does a second suspect who is fighting extradition from Croatia.
Kuznetsov became the first suspect to go on trial for the blasts on Wednesday morning, and a packed public gallery looked on as he entered the courtroom, appearing relaxed.
He even smiled at times, including during initial exchanges where he spoke to confirm personal details such as his name and place of birth.
He had previously only been identified by German prosecutors as Serhii K and pictured with his face blurred, but a court spokeswoman said he had now waived his anonymity.
Kuznetsov, 50, wore a pair of headphones and appeared to listen intently to a translation of proceedings in Ukrainian, as the prosecution read out the charges against him of ordering divers and an explosive expert to attack civilian infrastructure.
The defence outlined their case, telling the court that only circumstantial evidence had emerged in the four years since the Nord Stream blasts.
"[Prosecutors] made a thorough investigation of four years," Italian defence lawyer Nicola Canestrini told the BBC outside the courtroom. "They did not find one single witness, they did not find no forensics, no DNA, no fingerprints - nothing!"
Kuznetsov was extradited to Germany from Italy late last year
Canestrini and his colleagues argued that as a soldier the defendant was bound to secrecy, and therefore he could not have a fair trial as he was unable to defend himself.
"Let's say he has an alibi, he was on another secret operation, how can you prove that if he's [not able] to tell us as defence attorneys where he was and which witnesses we could summon?"
Prosecutors argue the case falls under Germany's code of crimes against international law as a war crime, as an "attack by military means against civilian objects".
The defence told the court his extradition to Germany was flawed as no mention had been made at the time of the war crime allegation.
In the months after explosives destroyed three of the four gas pipelines in the Baltic Sea off the island of Bornholm on 26 September 2022, Western suspicion looked towards Moscow without directly apportioning blame.
Russia had already shut off the flow of gas to Germany in Nord Stream 1 weeks before the attack, and Nord Stream 2 had never been turned on. Berlin had frozen the multi-billion dollar project shortly before the invasion and there were reports of suspicious Russian naval movements before the blasts.
As investigators from Sweden, Denmark and Germany tried to find out who carried out the attack, Russia's Vladimir Putin accused the US and its UK allies, blaming "the Anglo-Saxons" - which they denied.
Eventually, after Denmark and Sweden shut down their inquiries, German prosecutors focused on a group of deep-sea divers who had rented a yacht called the Andromeda in the northern German port of Rostock.
They said later that  "traces of subsea explosives were found in the samples taken from the boat".
Despite the strain on relations with Kyiv, German prosecutors pressed ahead with the case, and in January 2025the German federal court of justice ruled that it fell within German territorial jurisdiction,externaland prosecutors had a responsibility to act as it involved "undermining [Germany's] internal security".
Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky has always maintained that Ukraine had "nothing to do with [the Nord Stream blasts]", although in their indictment German prosecutors allege the saboteurs conceived the plot "acting by order of Ukrainian state agencies".
Nord Stream trial: How German police followed the evidence - to Ukraine
The case has highlighted differences of opinion on the trial in Kyiv and Berlin.
Oleksandr Merezhko, who chairs the Foreign Affairs Committee in the Ukrainian parliament, points out that the blasts took place during a time of war with Russia and "Nord Stream 2 was nothing but a tool used by Russia in order to get prepared for the war".
He told the BBC they had no confirmation of the German account: "It's one of the versions."
However, Stefan Meister, of the German Council on Foreign Relations, says successive chancellors in Berlin have done their best to remove the politics from the case.
"They tried to make not a big story out of it, not to give it too much attention, to give it to the institutions, to the judiciary that they will deal with it. This is not a political case. So they tried to depoliticise it," he explained.
Three of the four Nord Stream pipelines were ruptured by explosions in September 2022
In August 2025, Kuznetsov was arrested after checking into a hotel near the Italian Adriatic resort of Rimini, by police acting under a European arrest warrant issued by federal prosecutors in Germany.
After several weeks of court battles fighting extradition, when his surname emerged in court documents, Kuznetsov was transferred to Germany late last year.
German prosecutors allege that in 2022he was a serving officer in the Ukrainian army,external, and he had led a group of professional divers, a boat captain and an explosives expert.
While his legal fight was going on in Italy, another Ukrainian man called Volodymyr Zhuravlov successfully challenged Germany's extradition bid in a Polish court.
In a ruling very different from Italy's Supreme Court, the Polish judge ordered Zhuravlov's release in October 2025, stating that the attack on the pipelines was not unlawful, and if Ukraine had organised an armed mission it was "justified, rational and just".
Although he was released by the court in Warsaw, he was arrested last August in Croatia on suspicion of being a suspect who "participated in the dives necessary" for the sabotage.
Last month, Croatia approved his extradition, although it is not clear when that will happen, and if his case could become part of the Hamburg trial.
Despite the difficult nature of the case for Kyiv and Berlin, Ukrainian MP Oleksandr Merezhko does not believe it will spoil relations as "it's in the best national interests of Germany to continue to support us".

title: Drop-off charges at UK airports to be reviewed after sharp increase
summary: Confirming the review, the government said it was "vital to ensure travel remains accessible and that passengers are treated fairly".
body:
Airport drop-off charges are to be reviewed by the government following sharp price increases in recent years.
Prices at major UK airports have risen by a third since the summer of 2025 on average, according to one analysis, with Gatwick and Stansted drop-off charges found to be the most expensive, jumping from £7 to £10.
Such charges at Edinburgh Airport have risen from £6 to £8.50, while fees at Bournemouth increased from £5 to £8, the same price as Leeds Bradford and London City.
The Department for Transport confirmed it had committed to a review, saying it was "vital to ensure travel remains accessible and that passengers are treated fairly".
The government added it hoped airports would "exercise restraint on rises, particularly where there are limited public transport alternatives".
The RAC, which conducted the analysis in July this year, has campaigned against increases in drop-off charges. It said a review of "kiss and fly" fees would be "music to the ears to drivers".
"We know airport drop-off charges are a growing source of anger and frustration," said Rod Dennis, senior policy officer at the RAC.
"Four-in-five drivers we've surveyed believe they are a 'rip-off', with just one-in-10 understanding why airports charge what they do."
The RAC's research found London City Airport, which only introduced charges in 2026, was the most expensive on a per-minute basis.
Its £8 charge for five minutes works out at £1.60 per minute. Belfast International Airport now charges £5 for 10 minutes in the drop-off zone, up £2 on last year.
None of the top 10 airports in the European Union charge for drop-offs, according to the RAC.
It argues that international airports should not charge for dropping off passengers, however, the industry said the charges were a neccesary part of the business model of airports.
Airport drop-off fees up by a third - here are the priciest
Supporters of such charges also say they encourage travellers to use of more environmentally friendly modes of transport.
"Airports outside the UK are typically publicly owned and in receipt of state subsidies and tax exemptions, while UK airports are generally privately owned and subject to the full array of commercial rates of taxation," said Karen Dee, chief executive of Airports UK, which represents airports.
She added airports offered a "range of options for those travelling to terminals, including free drop off points" and that "any review" by the government would find airports make "excellent use of a variety of ways to manage traffic and air pollution".
The Aviation Environment Federation campaign group has previously defended the fees, arguing they help reduce congestion and air pollution around airports.
Earlier this month, the government announced extra charges for parents sitting with their children when flying would be scrapped in time for next year's summer holidays.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the changes were part of a series of "everyday fixes" to ease cost of living pressures on households.

title: Netflix to shed 1,000 jobs in steepest cuts since 2022
summary: The cuts equate to around 6% of the streaming giant's total workforce worldwide.
body:
Netflix has said it will cut 1,000 jobs globally as the streaming giant faces competition from rivals.
The cuts - the steepest since 2022 - will mainly affect its human resources, legal, product and technology teams and equates to around 6% of its total workforce.
Last month, Netflix 's co-chief executive, Ted Sarandos, told the Bloomberg Screentime summit that the company was "not growing as fast as I want us to".
The streaming industry is going through a period of consolidation following Paramount's $110bn (£83.6bn) merger with Warner Bros, the owner of HBO, while free platforms such as YouTube and TikTok continue to attract viewers.
In an email to staff, Sarandos and co-chief executive Greg Peters said Netflix would "continue to invest aggressively in high-impact areas to improve our service and further drive growth and innovation".
Netflix had come close to its own deal with Warner Bros but wasoutbid in the end by Paramount.
Commenting on the "organisational changes", Sarandos and Peters said: "Our mission - to entertain the world - is ambitious, and delivering on it requires us to be disciplined about where we prioritise our people and resources."
Managers will tell employees whether their job has been cut "soon".
TV series Below, starring Josh Hartnett, is one of Netflix's most popular shows
The email added that the firm was on track to meet its financial forecasts. The streaming service is due to report its latest results on 20 October.
Investors have been weighing up user engagement - the amount of time customers spend on Netflix - as it competes with platforms such as YouTube and TikTok.
The firm has continued to commission shows - its most popular at the moment is "Below", an underwater mystery series.
It has also been attempting to expand its business, including gaming and allowing adverts to play before and during shows and films.
However, "they haven't been able to find another line of major revenue," said Ross Benes, senior analyst at eMarketer.
He added that the company remains reliant on a subscription business that could be approaching a plateau.
"Eventually, because they're nearing a ceiling with that, they'll need another revenue stream to diversify, and that's where it's been more of a struggle," he said.
The last major redundancy round at Netflix was in 2022, when it cut about 450 jobs after losing subscribers for the first time in more than a decade.

title: How backlash against data centres could shape the US midterm elections
summary: Democrats and Republicans alike are coming out against data centre development, amid growing backlash across the US.
body:
Watch: The BBC's Shaimaa Khalil is in Arizona to hear from residents about the expansion of data centres.
A year ago, a longtime US senator was not thinking much about data centres. ​​
Now, according to one of his advisers, he is having regular meetings with staff to track their impact and working on new legislation aimed at curbing their rapid expansion across the country.
"This happens sometimes, something starts slow and then it goes fast", the senior policy adviser to the Democratic senator told the BBC. The person spoke on condition of anonymity as they are not permitted to speak to the press.
The 180-degree turn in this senator's attention was driven almost entirely by a growing wave of public backlash that has seen politicians across the country scramble to keep up. Public sentiment has turned against the expansion of data centres, the large warehouses that store processing power needed for internet activity.
Packed with rows and rows of computer chips, sometimes seven-feet high, data centres have turned into more than infrastructure for the internet. They are now the physical embodiment of the recent and explosive growth of artificial intelligence (AI) technology, and the varied fears people associate with it.
"I don't want to be the guinea pig for this," Indiana resident Angelita Soriano told the BBC.
A backlash over data centres is another threat to the AI juggernaut
A new Amazon data centre is being built directly across the street from her home. When complete, the 26-building structure will take up more than a square mile in her neighbourhood and maintain 782 diesel-powered generators.
Some data centres are even larger. In Ohio, a joint effort between OpenAI, Nvidia, SB Energy and the US Department of Energy is set to build a data centre complex that will stretch for roughly six square miles, the same size as most townships in the US.
There are about 3,000 data centres currently operating in the US, with that number potentially doubling in the next few years, according toa report by,externalPew Research Center.
Data centres are built through very local rules and permits, meaning federal lawmakers like US senators have little say in the process.
Yet, opposition has become so strong so quickly in the US that suddenly, politicians at all levels are now all but required to take a stand.
"This isn't just an issue on the left, there is huge pushback among conservatives to data centres," Chloe Autio, an AI policy adviser, said. "Whoever articulates a clear position and sticks to it, in either party, really stands to benefit."
Her analysis was echoed by the adviser to the US Senator working on data centre legislation.
"There is a clear policy need here that we're looking to fill," he said. "This is a major backlash across the country - constituents are seeing the impacts of data centres and they do not like them."
That has put many on Capitol Hill - even Republicans - in direct conflict with President Donald Trump, who has championed the unrestrained growth of AI technology.
Trump has dubbed the backlash to data centres a "sick conspiracy" and said people and towns working to keep the buildings out are "backwards and poor".
His ire has been used as a boon to Democratic politicians looking to draw midterm votes from unhappy or undecided constituents.
The BBC spoke to residents of Indiana, Arizona, Michigan, Pennsylvania and Oregon, all of whom have been organising locally against the development of data centres. They expressed concerns about many aspects of the buildings, including their size, construction and operational noise, their impact on air, water and energy resources, as well as the speed at which they seem to be approved by local authorities.
During the first few months of this year, community groups organising against data centres more than doubled to 833, cropping up in almost every US state, according to research from Data Center Watch. The firm collects data for AI industry stakeholders and is part of an AI startup 10a Labs.
Stephanie Maldonado, the political director of LUCHA, a community organising group based in Arizona, referred to the push back against data centres as "a David and Goliath story" that began several years ago.
"People have been ready to put a stop to it," Maldonado added. "Now, people are angry."
New national polling,externalshows that AI regulation and data centres are among some of the top issues for voters this election cycle, behind the ongoing Iran War and various aspects of the economy.
Proponents of building data centres often argue the projects will create more, and better paying, local jobs.
Yet,recent research,externalfrom Brookings Institution, a non-partisan policy research group, found that a new data centre creates between 100 and 200 local jobs, which is "fewer than industry advocates claim". The projects also have essentially no impact on local wages.
LUCHA, a community organising group based in Arizona, has made stopping data centre development one of their key issues
Arizona Governor Katie Hobbs was one such proponent - until public pressure pushed her to the other side of the issue. In July, she enacted a three-year pause on any new tax break given to a company for a data centres project.
Arizona is far from the only state to see politicians react to data centre backlash.
Abdul El Sayed, a Democrat running for Senate in Michigan, made new rules and regulations for data centres a clear part of his successful primary campaign for Senate.
In the race for governor of Georgia, a Democrat who is calling for a pause on data centre development is in a dead heat with a Republican who disagrees.
Republican Senator John Husted of Ohio, who is fighting to keep his seat against Democrat Sherrod Brown, has also had to shift his position.Recent polls,externalhave found that the majority of Ohio voters oppose data centres. He has softened his support, saying that their arrival should be up to local citizens and elected officials.
Meanwhile, Brown has stumped on his opposition to new data centres. He leads Husted in recent polls.
Husted's trouble in Ohio led the National Republican Senatorial Committee, the major fundraising arm for conservatives in the Senate, to write in aprivate memo,externalthat Republican politicians needed to entirely reframe how they spoke to voters on data centres.
"This has become a sleeper issue for the entire election cycle", the NRSC added.
Texas is perhaps the most clear cut example of how backlash has turned into an undeniable issue for even the most pro-business politician.
The state currently has almost 300 operational data centres, with another 170 planned for development, according to Pew data.
At the end of last year, Republican Governor Greg Abbott had boasted of Texas as "the epicentre of AI development" because of the number of data centres it housed.
Within months he was backtracking, citing concerns of "safety and quality of life".
It could play a part in the state's upcoming senate race too.
Democrat James Talarico's campaign is pushing for an end to "sweetheart tax deals" for Big Tech. He's now seen as a frontrunner for the historically Republican seat, where he is facing off against Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton.
Paxton said in a late September interview that there was still "plenty of open space in Texas that we can put data centres".
Democrat James Talarico has made data centres a part of his campaign for Senate
Many of the actions or proposals that have come from politicians looking to appease or address these voters are temporary. Most of the moratoriums, for instance, will end in one to three years.
It is possible that the political winds will have shifted by the time such moratoriums expire, leaving Big Tech and AI firms to build as they wish.
For now, people's feelings toward them are strong.
Balaji Tammabattula, the chief executive of Barupon, is developing a roughly 700-acre data centre and technology campus in Liberty, Texas. Despite the buildings being designed to use rain capture for water and supply its own energy needs, an increasingly common design for major data centre projects, Tammabattula told the BBC that people in the community oppose the project out of hand.
"There's just such a high level of tension from the jump that you can't really even break through with the facts," he said.
During a recent community event, Tammabattula said he tried to speak one-on-one with a woman who was vociferously opposed to the project.
"She just looked right at me and said, 'Get the hell out of my state.'"

title: Toilet paper and secret recorders: What we know about the arrest of the Saudi OpenAI engineer
summary: Abdulrahman Alfozan had worked for the AI giant for more than a year before he was arrested by the FBI.
body:
A recording device (R) was wrapped in toilet paper and plugged into a TV (L)
A Saudi national who worked for OpenAI appeared in court this week for allegedly planting a secret recording device behind a TV in one of the tech giant's meeting rooms.
Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old engineer, was arrested by the FBI and charged with using or attempting to use a device "to intercept oral communications".
As yet, it is not clear what he was planning to do with the recordings.
But, here's wedoknow so far.
The engineer asked AI to help him listen in to discussions about AI, according to an official complaint (the document filed in court).
Between 17 August and 16 September, Alfozan had reportedly asked a productivity AI assistant several questions about meeting rooms and their availability.
Some detailed in the complaint include "how about external partners, where would they usually meet with OpenAI at" and "can you list today's meeting in this room".
The complaint also claimed that in September, Alfozan used a chatbot associated with his spouse to ask how to build and install a recording device and how to access it remotely.
Alfozan had worked at the firm for around a year before he allegedly made his attempt to plant a recorder.
The room where the device was found was regularly used to hold meetings to discuss "highly confidential technical, commercial and strategic information" as well as OpenAI's "government engagements and commercial relationships", the complaint stated.
Alfozan had no authority to access or be involved with meetings in the room, the complaint states.
But CCTV footage recorded him near the conference room on eight separate occasions in September.
On 30 September, OpenAI staff discovered a "surreptitious audio recording device" behind a television - which had been wrapped in toilet paper.
A camera was placed in the conference room and on 5 October, Alfozan was filmed entering the room and appeared to look behind the television where the device had been inserted.
The complaint also stated that same day he allegedly left an unattended bag in a different room.
When security personnel opened it, it was found to contain "another recording device" similar to the one discovered, as well as Alfozan's wallet and ID.
In apost on X,external, OpenAI wrote it had used its own AI models to "understand the device and where it had come from".
It also said: "At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data."
Alfozan was captured looking behind a television where a device had been inserted
Alfozan had been employed as an engineer by OpenAI since July 2025. The complaint said he was educated in the US and has been a legal permanent resident since 2020.
He was arrested by the FBI on 9 October and his contract with OpenAI has been terminated.
Alfozan's lawyer William Pernik told the BBC: "Like countless Americans, Mr Alfozan came to this country years ago as a young person with a dream.
"These allegations appear wholly out of character for him, and we will relentlessly investigate all evidence produced by the government in this case to understand what actually happened, who was responsible and any possible reasons why."
Pernik added: "In the meantime, we respectfully ask everyone to withhold judgment until full facts become known. Like every one of us, Mr Alfozan is presumed innocent, and what has been made public is an accusation, not a finding of guilt."
On Tuesday, Alfozan made his initial appearance in a federal court in California. A detention hearing is scheduled on 19 October to determine whether he should remain in custody while proceedings continue.
The FBI investigation is ongoing.
If convicted, Alfozan faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison and a $250,000 (£190,000) fine.

title: Faisal Islam: What surprise praise for UK economy tells us about the Budget
summary: On three occasions in the past 24 hours, top IMF officials have praised UK plans to reduce its annual levels of borrowing.
body:
The managing director of the IMF, Kristalina Georgieva, has praised the UK's approach to debt reduction.
"Get your fiscal health in order," is a key message at the International Monetary Fund's (IMF) annual meeting here in Thailand.
The IMF is worried about the debts of the world's biggest economies. It is doing its job as a watchdog, looking for and warning about financial vulnerabilities.
In the meantime, the finance ministers of former crisis countries are boasting about how little their borrowing costs have gone up, compared to the world's biggest economies, such as the US.
On three occasions in the past 24 hours, top IMF officials havepraised the UK's plansto reduce its annual levels of borrowing, bucking the trend of the rest of the G7 group of countries, which includes Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the US.
The IMF clearly seeing the UK in a different light to these major economies is very interesting.
"The UK is actually one country where action to reduce debt and deficit has been taken decisively and we see the UK in that sense enjoying a bit of a better growth prospect,"  managing director Kristalina Georgieva said earlier.
Her comments followed those of the IMF's chief economist Silvana Tenreyro who told me that UK borrowing reductions "stand out".
Three things we've learnt about the UK economy from the IMF
UK growth forecast upgraded but higher energy prices to hit economy next year
The IMF's twice-yearly assessment of global countries' economic prospects showed only the UK among the G7 having a serious plan for consolidation of its annual borrowing over the next few years, worth nearly 4% of the size of the economy. The US, Germany and Japan are increasing borrowing. Canada and Italy are keeping borrowing at the same level.
It appears the UK is now the IMF's model pupil - at the top of the G7 table for reducing deficits.
This matters because for the past half decade the UK has been on the bond market naughty step, often having the highest borrowing rates among the G7 since the Liz Truss mini budget, as political and economic crises afflicted different governments.
While this is good news for the chancellor and the Treasury, it also points to the sort of Budget we will get in a fortnight's time. To keep its plans to reduce debt on track, John Healey is likely to have limited room for extra spending. He will want to marry this with limited tax rises. There could be a modest decrease in the margin for error around meeting debt rules - so-called headroom. If so that will be tied to providing a cushion against an expected rise in energy prices due to the ongoing Middle East conflict and the impact on the cost of living overall - the so called global inflation shock.
This is likely to mean disappointment for many public services expecting cash injections to account for rising inflation, as suggested this week by think tank the Institute for Fiscal Studies. It will mean tough public sector pay discussions.
It won't be "austerity" but the chancellor is likely to lean into the IMF framing of a government with austere plans, relative to other advanced countries. The initial prize is to avoid the direct gaze of the bond markets, whose full glare is on others, such as France now. The bigger prize could be lower relative borrowing costs for government and households.
Ultimately forecasts mean nothing without the underpinning of solid plans. Those plans will be here for everyone to judge soon enough.

title: We are behind you and that will not change, PM tells Zelensky
summary: The Ukrainian president visited London in an effort to bolster support among European allies following a row with Donald Trump.
body:
Why Zelensky's meeting with Burnham matters
"We are behind you and that will not change," Andy Burnham has told Volodymyr Zelensky, as he hosted the Ukrainian leader in Downing Street.
Zelensky was in London as part of efforts to reinforce backing from allies after Donald Trump called for him to go and lifted sanctions on Russian diesel.
The prime minister said Ukraine was willing to discuss an energy ceasefire proposed by the US president but said Russia's response had been "further attacks on critical national infrastructure in Ukraine".
Zelensky said: "Our people, we survived and continue to do this because we have strong partners and I'm very proud that we have one of the strongest partners in our history and it's your people, Andy."
The Ukrainian president was greeted with a hug from Burnham, cheers from civil servants and a rare honour guard as he arrived in Downing Street.
Ahead of Zelensky's arrival, No 10 announced it would speed up delivery of lightweight multirole missiles to Ukraine, which have been used to bring down Russian drones.
Burnham careful as he meets Zelensky but promises Ukraine won't leave 'empty handed'
Starlink restrictions in Ukraine war linked to political situation, Zelensky aide says
Russia's offensive ability is broken, Kyiv's former top general tells BBC
Ukrainian officials have said that overnight strikes by Russian missiles and drones had left at least 600,000 people without electricity.
For the second consecutive night, Ukraine said it had not received advanced warning from its allies of a wave of missile strikes coming from Russia.
Zelensky has suggested the US had threatened to restrict intelligence-sharing unless he agreed to sign up to an energy ceasefire. Trump has denied the US is holding back information.
An adviser to the presidenthas also saidUkraine's ability to defend itself from incoming missiles has been hindered by disruptions to its connection with the Starlink internet network, owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX company.
Serhiy Beskrestnov said the move "cannot be a coincidence and is related to the current political situation". The firm has not commented.
Speaking in Downing Street, Burnham said the recent days had been "dark and difficult" for Ukraine, with the country suffering "heavy bombardment".
He told the Ukrainian leader: "You have seen the solidarity and the support you have got from everybody here in Britain.
"We are behind you and that will not change."
Earlier in the day, Burnham had been invited to criticise the US decision to lift sanctions on Russia, when, at Prime Minister's Questions, Lib Dem leader Sir Ed Davey asked if the PM agreed there had been a "shameful Trump betrayal".
Burnham acknowledged that Zelensky was "carrying the heaviest of weights" but avoided attacking Trump, instead telling MPs that his role was to "repair bridges so that the support comes back".
"Therefore I should, at this moment in time, be careful in terms of laying the ground to bring people back together."
He added that Zelensky would not come away from his trip "empty-handed".
In a statement following the meeting, a Downing Street spokeswoman said the leaders had discussed "Russia's blatant indiscriminate attacks on civilians and energy infrastructure".
She said the prime minister promised that the UK would continue to develop "innovative military solutions for use on the battlefield in Ukraine, including retrofitting British capability onto equipment gifted from other partners".
The King held an audience with President Zelensky at Buckingham Palace as part of his visit to the UK
On Friday, Trump shocked European allies when he announced that he had reached a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to release an initial 300,000 tonnes of diesel, with more to follow.
Concerns about the cost of living are playing a key part in the US's November elections and the US president hopes his deal with Russia will reduce the cost of diesel.
The agreement runs counter to sanctions imposed on Russia by the US and its allies in a bid to choke off funds for Putin's war in Ukraine.
The deal came days after Trump accused Zelensky of wanting to "make problems for the world" and that it was time for Ukraine to "get a new president".
The criticism marks a renewal of Trump's previous hostility towards Zelensky which resulted in an infamous public row between the two men in the Oval Office.

title: Reform faces criticism after councillors filmed making racist comments
summary: Reform says all of those people filmed by ITV are under investigation having resigned or been suspended.
body:
Warning: This report contains racist and offensive language.
Reform UK has said "there is no room for racism" in its party after ITV News broadcast undercover filming, gathered over a year, of some of its councillors and candidates using racist, violent and sexist language.
In the film,Undercover: A Year in Reform,,externala Reform councillor and deputy mayor of Solihull is recorded calling Asian homeowners "parasites".
Labour described the investigation as "truly sickening" adding: "Nigel Farage can't shrug these latest revelations off as being a few bad apples."
A Reform spokesman said: "Where members, activists and councillors have clearly behaved inappropriately, investigations have commenced" and that in some cases there had been suspensions.
The spokesman added that the party had improved its procedures but some individuals who did not share their values would occasionally make it through vetting.
ITV's filming involved eight figures in Reform – the BBC does not know how many it spoke to in total.
Reform says the people filmed by ITV are all under investigation, and have already either resigned or been suspended.
ITV News says it had reporters undercover with Reform UK candidates and councillors across England and Wales running up to the elections in May and four by-election campaigns this year and last.
These reporters joined a Reform councillor, Alan Feeney, in Solihull, in the West Midlands, where he was campaigning to retain his seat on the council, having defected from the Conservative Party in 2025.
He told undercover reporters the area has been "infested" with Asian families, and called them "absolute parasites".
Later in the film, he is recorded saying: "I'd be saying no more than one per cent of British population can be non-white."
The BBC has tried to contact Feeney for a response.ITV has reportedthat on Monday evening he had "mutually agreed" to resign from Reform UK, citing "personal reasons," and would be continuing as an independent councillor.
Reform Party leader Nigel Farage has repeatedly said he wants to get rid of those he has called "bad apples."
Two years ago he said he didn't want Reform to be "a sectarian or racially based party in any way at all".
"I'm going to be absolutely ruthless about it," he said.
In a statement released after ITV's film was broadcast, Reform said the party "had improved and prioritised its vetting procedures, but from time to time, a handful of individuals who do not share our values will initially make it through vetting".
The Conservatives said: "Nigel Farage promised to make Reform ready for government. These sorry individuals are proof he has failed."
Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said: "This is chilling. I feel for anyone watching this tonight who is frightened to see such racism and hatred festering in their community."
A Green Party spokesman said: "Vilifying migrants and Muslims is Reform's main focus, and these racist comments reflect party policy."

title: Burnham had two hospitality dinners with Man City chairman, deleted records show
summary: The prime minister has been under growing pressure since the club was found guilty of Premier League rule breaches.
body:
Man City chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak (left) chats to Andy Burnham in 2019 at the Etihad Stadium, when he was mayor of Greater Manchester
Andy Burnham had two hospitality dinners with Manchester City football club's chairman while mayor of Greater Manchester, it has emerged.
The PM dined with Khaldoon Al Mubarak at matches in 2017 and 2018 - but this was not detailed in a statement on Monday by the Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA) about his meetings with the club.
Burnham has been under pressure to clarify his previous discussions with Man City since the club was found guilty of having "systematically" broken Premier League rules, which it will appeal.
The PM, who was mayor until June,sparked widespread controversywhen he said last month he would be "really concerned" if the club's owners now sold up.
On Monday, the GMCA released a statement about Burnham's meetings with Man City in his role as mayor for the region for almost a decade.
The statement said he had a formal meeting with Al Mubarak in October 2021 at the UK Government's Global Investment Summit, arranged by the Department for International Trade; and that he met the club chairman "informally in the stands" at a testimonial match in 2019 for former player Vincent Kompany.
It also said that "in his capacity as mayor, he was a guest of Manchester City at home matches on a small number of occasions".
But the statementdid not specify that this referred to,externaltwo hospitality dinners he had with the Manchester City chairman at separate matches.
A previous GMCA register of declarations for Burnham, seen by the BBC, detailed a "dinner with [then-Manchester City Council leader] Richard Leese and Chair of Man City" for an Everton match at the Etihad stadium in August 2017, valued at £300 for hospitality.
Below is another entry for "dinner with the Chairman at the Man City/Man Utd derby at the Etihad" in April 2018, valued at approximately £699.
Burnham previously declared those dinners, alongside a £150 pair of tickets to see Ed Sheeran perform at the stadium in May 2018.
But the register of declarations has since been deleted from the GMCA website, as first reported by The Sun. The BBC understands it is the authority's policy to only publish entries from the current mayoral term.
Man City guilty of 'sham' contracts and misleading accounts
BBC News has asked GMCA for more details about this policy - given its website has entries dating back to 2022, despite the current mayoral term beginning in 2024.
Downing Street has defended the two dinners with Man City's chairman, saying this was hospitality received at home games, which had been declared, rather than separate meetings with the club chairman.
But political pressure on Burnham to be clearer about any former discussions with Man City is continuing to mount.
Tory shadow sports minister Louie French said: "Andy Burnham promised the country and House of Commons full transparency on his dealings with Manchester City.
"This was essential after his inappropriate intervention into football."
And Reform UK's Robert Jenrick said "this saga stinks" as he accused Burnham of having apparently "concealed his extensive links to Man City's owners".
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has demanded for several days that No 10 release all details of meetings between the prime minister and senior figures at the club.
Burnham told the Rest Is Politics podcast last week he was "happy" to do this and would "quite clearly put out there everything that I have done working with them in my previous role as Mayor of Greater Manchester".
"None of it is recent, actually, in terms of the meetings I had. I only had one significant meeting, actually, and that was in 2021."
Asked at Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday whether anyone at the club had raised the charges they were facing with him or his team, Burnham said: "They did not raise those issues with me."
With the PM continuing to face pressure on the issue, he told MPs he was happy for "everything to be set out in full", referring to the GMCA's statement as "a full statement of my key dealings with the owners of Manchester City Football Club".
When asked by reporters why the statement did not refer to the two dinners, and what the difference is between "everything" and "key dealings", the PM's press secretary referred back to the GMCA statement.
The list of meetings, which was published by the GMCA on Monday, did not include detail on what was discussed. The BBC has asked GMCA why the two dinners were not specifically mentioned.
In September Man City - which has dominated the top flight of English football for years - was found guilty by an independent commission of breaching Premier League financial regulations.
The commission found City had broken rules over a nine-year period between 2009 and 2018 bycreating "sham" contracts with commercial partnersto secretly funnel more than £830m into their football operations.
Sanctions are yet to be announced and City, which denies any wrongdoing, has lodged an appeal against the verdict.
Earlier this month, Sir Richard Leese - who was head of Manchester City Council for 25 years until 2021 -defended a decade-old dealbetween the council and Man City owners Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG).
Under the partnership between the authority and the company, which is linked to the United Arab Emirates royal family, land was leased to ADUG at "below comparable rates", according to a University of Sheffield report.

title: UK threatens to ban Eritreans over migrant return policy
summary: The home secretary said she would not hesitate to impose measures on other countries "refusing to co-operate".
body:
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has threatened to ban all Eritreans from entering the UK if the east African country's government does not accept more returns of small boat migrants and foreign national offenders.
From Thursday, Eritrean diplomats will face restrictions on their movement outside London. Fast-track visas will also be stopped for VIPs.
Ministers have previously pressured other countries into accepting returns by threatening visa bans.
Eritreans were the most common nationality among small boats migrants in the 12 months to June -accounting for 18% of arrivals,external, according to figures from the House of Commons Library.
The Eritrean embassy in London has been contacted for comment.
"Eritrea has had every chance to accept the return of criminals and those with no right to be in the UK. Unlike other countries, it has refused," said Mahmood.
She said she would not hesitate "to impose further measures on other countries refusing to co-operate".
The UK government accused the Eritrean authorities of "abruptly" withdrawing co-operation earlier this year.
The restrictions mean diplomats are banned from travelling 60km outside London without permission.
The Home Office said this mirrored restrictions on British officials in Eritrea's capital Asmara.
Earlier this year, the UK threatened bans against Angola, Namibia and the Democratic Republic of  Congo (DRC).
Restrictions wereannounced against the DRClast year, but the Home Office said these have beenlifted after co-operation on returnsimproved.
Angola and Namibia both agreed changes before restrictions were introduced.
When announcing changes to the UK's asylum system in November, Mahmood said visa penalties would be applied to countries that failed to co-operate with returns policies.
Penalties included an "emergency brake" on visas for countries with high asylum claims until they take back citizens in the UK illegally.
According to Home Office data, more than 20,400 people have arrived in the UK by small boats so far since the beginning of this year, down 40% from the same period last year.
There were more than 40,600 returns and deportations from the UK from July 2025 to June this year - an 8% increase on the same period last year.
Of those who had been returned, less than 6,000 has been convicted of a criminal offence.

title: Burnham rules out coalition with Greens after 'Zionism is racism' motion
summary: Andy Burnham condemns the motion approved by Green Party members and says his party would "have nothing to do with it".
body:
Burnham condemns Green Party's 'antisemitic' Zionism declaration
Andy Burnham has said he will not support his party forming a partnership with the Green Party as long as it maintains a policy of defining Zionism as a form of racism.
Speaking in the House of Commons, the prime minister said the motion, backed by Green members at its party conference earlier this month, was "wrong" and "antisemitic" and Labour would have "nothing to do with it".
The motion said Zionism was an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state in historic Palestine to the exclusion and/ or domination of the non-Jewish population".
It was criticised by Jewish groups, as well as four Green MPs and two former leaders, one of whom said it was "dangerous" and "divisive".
Party leader Zack Polanski has said the motion was "imperfect" and that he had wanted to see it amended.
However, he has defended the substantial part of the motion arguing that "the displacement and genocide of the Palestinian people is clearly underpinned by racist ideology" was "obvious". Israel has repeatedly denied its actions in Gaza amount to genocide.
The motion, having been backed by members, has become party policy but will not necessarily be included in the party's manifesto at the next general election.
The subject was raised during Prime Minister's Questions, when Conservative MP Dame Harriett Baldwin urged Burnham to "rule out co-operating" with the Green Party.
Burnham replied: "Can I condemn the motion that was passed unequivocally.
"It is wrong, it is antisemitic, and this side of the House will have nothing to do with it.
"We will always take the right response when it comes to any partnerships we have with other parties.
"We cannot support a partnership with a party that holds the position that has recently been adopted."
In response to Burnham's comments, Polanski said: "I'm the only Jewish leader of a political party. I'm a victim of antisemitism every day and I've made it clear Jewish people are welcome in my party.
"You're a prime minister who arms a genocide and locks pensioners up for opposing it."
He added that the "blurring of challenging Israel and antisemitism" was "dangerous and irresponsible".
Labour is currently in coalition with the Green Party on local councils in Sheffield, Lewes and Warwick. In more than 10 other areas, Labour run the council with the Greens as part of a broader coalition.
A Downing Street spokesman would not confirm if the prime minister's position extended to local areas or just applied to national government level.
The adoption of the motion has prompted some Green Party figures to call for changes to the party's rules.
Last week, MP Ellie Chowns told the BBC: "I think it is clear that if we have policy, such significant and damaging policy, made by a vote of just 0.4% of our members, that something isn't working in our structures and our policy-making process."
Members of the Green Party of England and Wales endorsed the policy motion by 1,022 votes to 813 - a small fraction of the 230,000 members in the party.
Key backer of the motion Lubna Speitan has defended the motion arguing that it aimed to oppose "racist systems of oppression" adding: "We stand united against all forms of racism and discrimination - no exemptions."
